1.text:
'Alif-Lãm-Mĩm' is the full wording of this verse, three letters at the start of Surah Al-Imran. One view leaves their meaning with Allah alone. Another sees the disconnected letters as a challenge because the Qur'an is built from letters used in ordinary Arabic speech, yet its hearers cannot bring a book like it. This reading links the opening to the form of revelation rather than assigning a certain word to each letter. A spiritual reading treats the letters as allusions about sufficiency, kindness, and harmony. A source also preserves a report about the delegation of Najran and an oath affirming Allah’s oneness. These are distinct explanations, and the verse itself does not spell out a single lexical definition. The opening also belongs to the sequence of revelation after Al-Baqarah. The prayer at the end of Al-Fatihah asked for guidance to the straight path, and the account at the beginning of Al-Baqarah presents the Qur'an as that guidance. Al-Imran begins within the same discussion of the Book, while the surah's following verses move to Allah's Oneness and the scriptures revealed before the Qur'an. The short opening therefore marks the beginning of a new surah without closing the question of what each letter means.

**What the Letters Mean.**

Alif Lām Mīm God knows best what He means by these letters. It is said that by listening to these disconnected letters [Alif Lām Mīm] which are contrary to the ordinary customs of human discourse every concept disappears from the hearts whether it be a known written cus tomary or imagined thing and whether it arises from necessity Ḍarūra sensory perception ḥiss or independent reasoning ijtihād.

**Letters in the Qur’an.**

Alif Lām Mīm – the placement of such letters has been discussed at the beginning of Sūrah Al-Baqarah. They indicate the inability of the Arabs to bring a Qur’ān like this one despite the fact that it is composed of letters similar to the ones at the beginning of this Sūrah, which also form the parts of their own speech.

**What the Letters Allude To.**

Alif Lām Mīm His saying Alif alludes to His being sufficient for you in all of your states. He is the One who sets in motion what restores you and is solely sufficient for you in what helps you. Without your asking-and even without you knowing your own state-He suffices for you even if you do not perceive it. The Lām alludes to His kindness luṬf to you at the most subtle and hidden level so much so that the locus of favor by which He strengthens you is not apparent to you. The Mīm alludes to the harmony muwāfaqa of the stream of the [divine] determination of events taqdīr with the circumstances requested by the friends.

**Guidance from Earlier Surahs.**

It will be recalled that at the end of the Surah Al-Fatihah a prayer for guidance to the straight path was made. After that, by be-ginning the Surah Al-Baqarah with 1 ‌ (This Book which has no doubt in it), it was pointed out that the prayer made in Su-rah Al-Fatihah for guidance to the straight path has been accepted and Allah Almighty has sent down this Qur'an which provides guidance to the straight path.

**Guidance and Book.**

He has sent guidance for man throughout the ages, including the Torah and the Bible, which were revealed to the former prophets. Ultimately, in accordance with God’s plan, the final book in the form of the Quran was sent down to man. The Quran is not only a genuine book of guidance but also serves as the criterion or standard of right and wrong.

**Allah and an Oath.**

And on his authority he related from Ibn 'Abbas regarding the saying of Allah, Exalted is He: (Alif. Lam. Mim.) that he said: 'Allah informed us about the story of the delegation of Najran; it is also said that this is an oath by which Allah swore that He is One and that He has neither progeny nor partner. (Alif-Lam-Mim. Allah! None has the right to be worshipped but He, the Ever Living, the One Who sustains and protects all that exists.)

2.text:
'Allah! There is no god worthy of worship except Him, the Ever-Living, All-Sustaining' begins with absolute oneness and states that worship belongs to Allah alone. 'the Ever-Living' rules out death and deficiency, and 'All-Sustaining' names the One who exists without dependence and sustains every created thing. The attributes explain why none besides Him deserves worship. They are not only names but the basis of the declaration. The verse gives no partner or rival a share in worship, and it presents the Creator as the One on whom the whole creation depends. The following verse speaks of the Book revealed in truth, so the statement about Allah's life and sustaining power introduces the One who sends revelation and guides. 'There is no god' excludes every object of worship other than Him, while 'except Him' makes the affirmation exclusive. The names Ever-Living and All-Sustaining provide connected grounds for that exclusivity. He does not die or diminish, and His creation remains in need of Him. All creation remains dependent on Him, while He needs nothing from creation. The attributes describe the One who is self-subsisting and sustains creation, with no death or deficiency.

**The Ever-Living and Sustainer.**

In the words (Allah: there is no god but He) which follow immediately, the doctrine of the Oneness of Allah has been put forth as a categorical declaration. (Allah! None has the right to be worshipped but He, the Ever Living, the One Who sustains and protects all that exists) and,. (Allah! There is no God save Him, the Alive) Who dies not and is not evanescent, (the Eternal) the Self-subsistent Who has no beginning. Then come the words (the Alive, the All-Sustaining) which lay out a rational proof of the Oneness of Allah. The only Being worthy of worship is the One who has always been Alive and Present and shall always live and sustain.

**Worship Belongs to Him.**

It means that there is absolutely nothing worthy of worship other than Allah. (Alif-Lam-Mim. Allah! None has the right to be worshipped but He, the Ever Living, the One Who sustains and protects all that exists.) Therefore, it is crystal clear that all things in this world which have no power to come into being by themselves, nor can they sustain it - be they idols carved in stone, or water, or trees, or angels and apostles - none of them is worthy of worship. Allah is the One Who alone deserves to be worshipped. Bowing to the truth required them to bow to the Prophet and to God, and they thought that by surrendering to the Supreme Being and His Prophet they would diminish in stature.

**The Book That Follows.**

(It is He Who has sent down the Book to you with truth,) means, revealed the Qur'an to you, O Muhammad, in truth, meaning there is no doubt or suspicion that it is revealed from Allah. (In the Name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful)(1. Alif-Lam-Mim.)(2. Allah! None has the right to be worshipped but He, the Ever Living, the One Who sustains and protects all that exists.)(3. It is He Who has sent down the Book to you with truth, confirming what came before it. And He sent down the Tawrah and the Injil,)(4. Aforetime, as a guidance to mankind. 'Surely nothing on earth or in the heavens is hidden from Allah' leaves no place outside His knowledge. The verse names both earth and heaven and states that nothing in either is hidden. Its claim includes what people see and what they cannot see; Allah's knowledge is not bounded by human perception. It follows the account of revelation and the Standard: the One who sends guidance knows what is hidden from His servants and what they need. The next verse turns from what is hidden to Allah's shaping of people in the wombs as He wills. That sequence connects knowledge with creation; no hidden breath or unseen need is beyond Him. A servant may need what no one else perceives, but that need is not hidden from the One who creates and sustains all things. Even a breath is counted, and knowledge reaches before birth and after death, beyond what another person can observe. Allah's knowledge includes what is visible and what is hidden, and it is not limited by the senses.

**God's Knowledge of Heaven and Earth.**

Nothing no existent thing whatever is hidden in heaven and earth from God on account of His knowledge of universals and particulars. God specifies them heaven and earth because sensory perception does not go beyond these. Allah states that He has perfect knowledge in the heavens and earth and that nothing in them is hidden from His watch. He knows everything, whether it is open or hidden. Only God can truly tell us what He is in His Being and in His attributes. Not a particle exists in the heaven and earth unless He is its originator and creator mubdiʿ hi.

**Before Birth and After Death.**

And He has made this so clear in His Book, that any reader who is eager for knowledge of Him will certainly gain enlightenment from it. The right course of action for man can be determined only by a Being who has not only known man from his birth to his death, but also knows what has gone before his birth and what will happen after his death. It is, therefore, only God who, after placing the nature of man in the perspective of the entire universe, may decree what kind of conduct will guarantee man’s success in this world and the next, for a sound human mentality can only be one which is in harmony with the rest of the world and in complete accord with the vaster system of the cosmos. It is only God who has the power and the knowledge to ordain what it befits human beings to strive for in the present world. This being so, the only realistic approach for man is to trust in His Maker and accept and follow His guidance wholeheartedly and with full confidence. A servant does not breathe a single breath without God counting it muḥṣīhi.

'He is the One Who has revealed to you, O Prophet, the Book' identifies the One who sends revelation and the messenger who receives it. 'of which some verses are precise' points to clear statements whose meaning is established. 'they are the foundation of the Book' makes those verses the basis for reading the rest. 'while others are elusive' acknowledges passages whose full meaning is not immediately clear. 'Those with deviant hearts follow the elusive verses seeking to spread doubt through their false interpretations' shifts attention to the way a reader handles uncertainty: the aim is discord, not guidance. 'but none grasps their full meaning except Allah' sets a limit on what people can claim to know. Readers differ over the pause here: some stop at Allah, while others connect the well-grounded in knowledge with what follows. 'As for those well-grounded in knowledge, they say' introduces a response of humility rather than pursuit of confusion. 'We believe in this Quran' and 'it is all from our Lord' affirm the whole revelation, not only what is easy to understand. 'But none will be mindful of this except people of reason' closes by linking reflection with sound understanding. The verse does not license ignoring difficult passages; it directs interpretation back to the clear foundation and calls for faith where the full reality remains beyond human knowledge. The discussion also marks a limit: uncertainty is not permission to reject what the clear verses establish. One reading leaves the full interpretation with Allah alone; another joins those well-grounded in knowledge to the response that follows. In either case, the following words affirm that all the verses are from their Lord, and people of reason take admonition. The clear verses remain the reference point; interpretations of an elusive phrase that contradict them are rejected. Some readings call certain passages allegorical or leave their full reality to Allah, while the grounded affirm the entire Book. This restraint protects the message and the reader from turning uncertainty into discord. The following verse turns that posture into a prayer for hearts to remain firm.

The verse begins with what people love and ends with what is kept for them, and the order is the argument. "has been made appealing to people" turns to those who find them fair, and the wording does not name the one who made them fair, which is why the sources weigh two readings, that the adorning is from God as a test and that it comes from Satan, and they keep both because the verse does not settle it. "These are the pleasures of this worldly life" then gathers the whole list under one word and marks how long it lasts, since the comfort is taken and then goes. "but with Allah is the finest destination" ends on the contrast and leaves the better thing unnamed, so that the verse after it can set that out, and the abode with God is the one that remains. **The desire for women, children, and wealth.**

(Beautified for mankind is) what people's hearts find desirable is (love of the joys (that come) from women) meaning slave women and wives (and offspring) slaves and children, (and stored up heaps) amassed wealth (of gold and silver) it is also said that this means: minted or engraved gold and silver, (and horses branded (with their mark) beautiful branded horses and grazing in pastures, (and cattle) i.e. sheep, cows and camels (and land) cultivation and cultivated lands. Beautified for mankind is love of lusts that which the self lusts after and calls for beautified by Satan or by God as a test — of women children stored-up heaps of gold and silver horses of mark fine horses cattle namely camels cows and sheep and tillage the cultivation of land. **The love of the present life as a test.**

The list is not condemned for being loved. It is named as the field of a trial. Is it not that man, with love for these things in his heart, has been put to a test as to who becomes engrossed in the enjoyments of the present life and forgets the life to come, and who comes to realize the real and temporal nature of these things, shows concern for them only in proportion to his needs, and then channels all his efforts into deeds that would make his next life good and safe? God, wishing to ascertain which of His creatures are capable of rising above worldly attractions, has so willed it that man should be attracted to and find gratification in the things of this world, but at the same time be faced with the choice of clinging to them or renouncing them in favour of the unseen things of the next world. Sometimes, the want for more money is for the purpose of spending it on acts of worship, being kind to the family, the relatives, and spending on various acts of righteousness and obedience; this behavior is praised and encouraged in the religion.

All this is just to grab a share in the temporal enjoyments of the present life which has been described in these verses. Similarly, man's wealth and possessions are means of convenience for his role in this world and in the life to come - provided that they do not enter into his heart, sit there, and kill it in the process.

The verse stands at the head of the passage as the testimony on which everything after it rests, and it gives the witness first, then those who bear it with Him.
